This measurement illustrates the cosmic-ray muon angular dependence measured near sea level. Two detectors were operated in coincidence mode and positioned side-by-side (configuration (a) in Fig. ??), with their scintillators separated by 50 mm inside identical aluminum enclosures. The detector angle 𝜃 was set by mounting both units on a 40 cm rectangular bar and leaning the bar against a vertical wall at a known height (see Fig. 2.4, right). Fig. 2.4 (left) shows the measured rate as a function of zenith angle. Each data point represents approximately 24 hours of data, and the rate uncertainties are purely statistical.

In this configuration, the detectors are oriented to sample muons within ±20<sup>∘</sup> of the set angle. Several contributions to the measured rate are expected. First, the angular dependence of cosmic-ray muons at sea level follows a cosine-squared law, I(𝜃) ∝ cos<sup>2</sup>𝜃, where 𝐼(𝜃) is the differential muon intensity as a function of zenith angle 𝜃(with 𝜃= 0<sup>∘</sup> corresponding to vertically downward-going muons) \[?\]. Second, there is an accidental coincidence rate where 𝑁<sub>1</sub> = 3.3 Hz and 𝑁<sub>2</sub> = 2.9 Hz are the individual detector trigger rates, and 𝜏= 2.3 𝜇s is the coincidence window. Finally, extensive air showers produce muon bundles, multiple muons arriving simultaneously from a single primary cosmic-ray interaction, which can trigger both detectors, resulting in a higher coincidence rate at all angles. Figure 2.4 overlays the expected cos<sup>2</sup>𝜃 dependence and the flat accidental background rate, together with the remaining offset attributed to the air-shower contribution.

A slight increase in rate at 𝜃= 𝜋/2 is attributed to this configuration accepting muons from both upward and downward directions, whereas all other orientations record only downward-going muons. Therefore, the single-muon contribution at 𝜃= 𝜋/2 should, in principle, be halved.
